newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS-Bunds get a minor facelift from budget.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS-Bunds get a minor facelift from budget.

text.p: Germany's budget plans may give Bunds a winning edge over U.S. Treasuries but any mileage on the spread will be short-lived, economists said on Friday.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet on Friday approved Finance Minister Theo Waigel's 1998 draft budget, and a supplementary budget for 1997 that raises the projected deficit to 71.2 billion marks from an original 53.3 billion.
Economists are analysing whether the deficit will meet or come close to the 3.0 percent deficit/GDP ratio criterion for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"According to my calculations they will have 3.2 percent," said Gerhard Grebe, chief economist at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt.
"It could even be 3.0 percent," he said, adding Bonn's plans to redefine the public sector in line with the rest of Europe would further trim the gap.
But despite a Bund-friendly budget, economists were not convinced the ratio would be a clean 3.0 percent, and this would keep the domestic scene clouded.
Economic fundamentals would also favour Treasuries in the medium term, they said. German growth was expected to pick up, bringing inflation concerns back to the forefront.
"Near term there is potential for spread widening but in the medium term the risks are German yields will push higher," said Sonja Gibbs, senior bond strategist at Nomura International.
She forecast the 10-year T-note/Bund yield spread at 60 basis points by the end of September. Short-term, economists expect the gap to stretch to 90 from 80 now.
September Bund futures have mustered gains of nearly four points since the end of May, to touch a peak of 103.15 on Wednesday. By 1045 GMT, they stood at 102.84, up 0.13 on the day.
Economists see troubles continuing to dog the EMU agenda before its planned launch on January 1, 1999.
Opposition Social Democrats (SPD) have already attacked Waigel's budget, saying the government pushed higher debt burdens onto future generations.

"Whatever the details, the SPD are not going to agree to it straight off. The budgetary process is going to be a reasonably long one," said David Brickman, European economist at Yamaichi International Europe.
Also, a higher deficit suggests more bond supply, pushing German yields higher against their U.S. counterparts, he said.
Yet Bunds could outperform T-notes, Brickman said.
"There is no reason why we can't move to 5.25 percent in terms of 10-year Bund yields (from 5.55 now)," Brickman said.
"But one has to keep an eye on the U.S.. If we were to see a significant sell-off in Treasuries then Bunds would struggle to make absolute gains."

Julius Baer's Grebe, however, saw Bunds trailing T-notes in the autumn. "Growth is accelerating in Germany. In August we'll have the lowest inflation rate and then inflation will move upwards," he said.
Bunds were driven by high liquidity through low money market rates and a steep yield curve, but portfolio managers were nervous about the prospect of an interest rate hike.
"In the autumn it will become more evident that Bundesbank will raise rates in the first quarter of 1998," Grebe said.
Elsewhere, Bunds were likely to close the negative yield gap against OATs, which economists said survived with a favourable tax treatment on domestic investors in France.

"If we see a reversal of that then in the long term we will see a shift out of French bonds into equities by domestic investors," said Brickman. A decision is likely to be unveiled in a French state budget audit on July 21.
